Christian Magistrate
KRIS-chun MAJ-is-trayt
noun phrase (the civil ruler under God)
From “magistrate” (Latin magistratus, a public office); the civil ruler considered as a minister of God, accountable to rule justly and in the fear of God.

📖 Biblical Definition

The Christian magistrate is the civil ruler considered as a minister of God—the office of governing authority understood in the light of Scripture, accountable to the God who ordained it. The apostle teaches that the powers that be are ordained of God, and that the ruler is the minister of God for good, bearing the sword to execute wrath upon the evildoer; rulers are therefore not autonomous but stewards under a higher King. Scripture sets the standard for the office: “He that ruleth over men must be just, ruling in the fear of God”; and it pronounces that “righteousness exalteth a nation: but sin is a reproach to any people.” The church is charged to pray for kings and all in authority, that under good government it may lead a quiet and peaceable life in all godliness and honesty. The dictionary holds the civil magistrate to be a God-ordained authority within its proper sphere, distinct from the family and the church, owed honour and obedience in all things lawful. On the harder questions—how far the magistrate should establish or defend true religion, and the proper relation of church and state—the Reformed tradition has differed, the older establishment view (and Bucer's De Regno Christi) leaning on the godly prince, while the Baptist tradition, with the 1689 Confession, stresses liberty of conscience and the spiritual nature of Christ's kingdom. The dictionary marks the office against two errors: the statism that makes the government an idol owed unlimited obedience, when the magistrate is himself under God and may be disobeyed when he commands sin; and the antinomian or anarchic spirit that despises lawful authority, which Scripture commands the Christian to honour as ordained of God.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

The civil ruler as a minister of God, ordained within his proper sphere and accountable to rule justly in the fear of God (Romans 13:1; 2 Samuel 23:3); owed honour and lawful obedience, against both statist idolatry and anarchic contempt of authority.

CHRISTIAN MAGISTRATE, noun phrase. The civil ruler considered as a minister of God.

“The powers that be are ordained of God” (Romans 13:1).

“He that ruleth over men must be just, ruling in the fear of God” (2 Samuel 23:3).

The church is to pray for kings and all in authority (1 Timothy 2:2).

Owed honour and lawful obedience, yet himself under God and resistible when he commands sin.

📖 Key Scripture

Ro 13:1 — "Let every soul be subject unto the higher powers. For there is no power but of God: the powers that be are ordained of God."

1 Ti 2:2 — "For kings, and for all that are in authority; that we may lead a quiet and peaceable life in all godliness and honesty."

Pr 14:34 — "Righteousness exalteth a nation: but sin is a reproach to any people."

2 Sa 23:3 — "The God of Israel said, the Rock of Israel spake to me, He that ruleth over men must be just, ruling in the fear of God."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Statism makes government an idol owed unlimited obedience, forgetting the magistrate is under God; the anarchic spirit despises lawful authority Scripture commands the Christian to honour as ordained of God.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the magistrate as God's minister, neither an idol nor a nullity. The first corruption is statism: the making of government into a god owed unlimited and unconditional obedience. Scripture forbids this. The magistrate is ordained of God but is under God, a minister accountable to rule justly in His fear; when he commands what God forbids, the Christian must obey God rather than men. The state that claims the conscience claims what belongs to God alone.

The opposite corruption is the anarchic or antinomian contempt of authority that despises lawful rulers and counts submission beneath Christian liberty. But the apostle commands every soul to be subject to the higher powers, to honour the king, and to pray for all in authority. The dictionary holds the balance, while noting the Reformed family's long differences over the magistrate's role in religion—the older establishment view leaning on the godly prince, the Baptist tradition stressing liberty of conscience and the spiritual kingdom. On that the conscience is not here bound; but the abiding rule stands: honour the magistrate as ordained of God, obey him in all things lawful, resist him only where he commands sin, and remember that righteousness, not raw power, exalteth a nation.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

From the Latin magistratus (a public office or officer); the civil authority considered, with Romans 13, as a diakonos (minister) of God for good.

expand to see more

Magistratus, Latin, a public office or magistrate.

Exousiai, Greek, the “higher powers” ordained of God (Romans 13:1).

Diakonos Theou, “minister of God,” the ruler's title in Romans 13:4.

The “sword” he bears for justice, distinct from the church's spiritual power.

Distinguished from family and church as a separate God-ordained sphere.

Usage

"The pastor taught that the magistrate is God's minister, owed honour yet himself under God."

"He resisted the statism that claims the conscience, obeying God rather than men where they conflict."

"She prayed for kings and all in authority, that the church might lead a quiet and peaceable life."
